claim.pdf_says: 14.9.51.3   Syntax rules  (printed in the same bold sub-clause style as 14.9.51.1 General and 14.9.51.2 General formats on page 815)
claim.markdown_says: ## 14.9.51.3 Syntax rules   (H2, while its siblings on page 815 are '### 14.9.51.1 General' and '### 14.9.51.2 General formats')
claim.why_it_matters: A four-level clause number (14.9.51.3) is promoted to the same heading level as the statement clause itself (## 14.9.51 WRITE statement). The syntax rules stop being nested inside the WRITE statement clause, which breaks the document outline, any TOC generated from it, and any tooling that resolves a citation like '14.9.51.3' by walking the heading tree. ISO_COBOL.md line 33010 (and 33074 for 14.9.51.4, on a later page) carry the same defect.

verdict.reasoning: VERIFIED against the 300dpi renders of pages 816 and 815 and against specs/ISO_COBOL.md. Every literal fact in the claim checks out. Page 816 prints 'where retry-phrase is described in 14.7.9, RETRY phrase' followed by the bold sub-clause heading '14.9.51.3   Syntax rules', then numbered rules 1)-9). ISO_COBOL.md line 33010 reads '## 14.9.51.3 Syntax rules' (H2) and line 33074 reads '## 14.9.51.4 General rules' (H2), while lines 32941 and 32946 read '### 14.9.51.1 General' and '### 14.9.51.2 General formats' (H3) and line 32938 reads '## 14.9.51 WRITE statement' (H2). So 14.9.51.3 and .4 really are encoded as siblings of their own parent clause and as one level shallower than their own siblings .1 and .2. This is not a convention: the immediately preceding statement clause transcribes 14.9.50.3 and 14.9.50.4 as '###' (lines 32799, 32814), so the file contradicts itself inside a single statement. I attempted three refutations and all three failed. (1) 'The text is missing' -- it is not, but the claim never says it is missing despite the 'missing-heading' kind label; the heading text is present and matches the PDF verbatim, so nothing is lost, only mis-nested. (2) 'It is only formatting' -- rejected: in Markdown the '#' count is not styling, it is the sole encoding of nesting depth, and here it encodes a false statement about the standard's clause hierarchy (that Syntax rules is a peer of WRITE statement rather than a child). (3) 'The PDF gives no basis for a level distinction' -- I checked the printed glyphs on both pages: 14.9.51, 14.9.51.1, 14.9.51.2 and 14.9.51.3 are all set in the same bold face, same size, same left margin, so the print itself does not distinguish levels visually; the nesting is established purely by the dotted clause number, and 14.9.51.3 is unambiguously a child of 14.9.51. That confirms rather than refutes the claim. What the claim overstates is the consequence, and the scope is understated -- see corrected_description.
verdict.corrected_description: Real, but mislabeled and under-scoped. (a) The kind is not 'missing-heading' -- nothing is missing. The heading is present at ISO_COBOL.md:33010 with text matching the PDF exactly; the defect is a heading-LEVEL / nesting error ('wrong-heading-level'). (b) This is not a two-line local defect. It is one instance of a document-wide transcription pattern: 162 four-level clause headings in ISO_COBOL.md are emitted as '##' against 620 emitted as '###', spanning 6.2.3.2 through 16.2.1.2. The correct remedy is a single mechanical sweep normalizing every N.N.N.N heading to H3 (and re-checking the corresponding N.N.N and N.N depths), not a per-page edit of lines 33010 and 33074. (c) The stated impact is overstated on one point: citation resolution does not in fact break, because each heading carries an explicit anchor -- line 33009 is '' -- and anchors, not heading depth, are the resolution mechanism; furthermore the file already interleaves '## Page NNN' markers at H2 (e.g. line 32939 '## Page 816' region), so no consumer can be walking a pure clause tree in the first place. The genuine impact is narrower: a generated TOC/outline and any depth-based chunking that attributes rule text to its owning clause will place 14.9.51.3/.4 outside 14.9.51. (d) No normative content is affected -- the 9 syntax rules on page 816 transcribe correctly, including the rule 7) a)/b) sub-list. Severity is fairly 'structural' only in the markup sense; it is not a semantic divergence from the standard.
